title: Near-Optimal Dynamic Matching via Coarsening with Application to Heart Transplantation
claim: Aggregating offline nodes into capacitated clusters yields online matching performance far above the status quo policy.
layout: 2 panels, left schematic then right plot; donor-to-cluster arrows plus a line chart
description: The figure has two panels. On the left, a schematic shows a vertical time axis labeled 'Online donor arrivals'. Heart icons sit at times t1 to t4. Dashed lines link each arrival to a donor type box, either 'Donor type A' or 'Donor type B'. From the donor type boxes, arrows go to two circles labeled 'Patient cluster 1' and 'Patient cluster 2', each holding three blue dots for patients. Green arrows mark a 'High benefit' match, and gray crossing arrows are labeled 'Incompatible'. On the right, a line plot shows competitive ratio (y-axis) against minimum cluster size b (x-axis). A solid blue curve for 'Our algorithm' rises quickly and levels at about 0.88 to 0.9. It has a shaded confidence band. A dashed red 'Status quo' line stays flat at about 0.51. The large gap between the two lines draws the eye first.
caption: Left: Schematic illustration of our coarsening-based approach. Right: Competitive ratio of our algorithm compared against the post-2018 US status quo allocation for different budgets $b$ evaluated in simulation from January to June 2019.
abstract: Online matching has been a mainstay in domains such as Internet advertising and organ allocation, but practical algorithms often lack strong theoretical guarantees. We take an important step toward addressing this by developing new online matching algorithms based on a coarsening approach. Although coarsening typically implies a loss of granularity, we show that, to the contrary, aggregating offline nodes into capacitated clusters can yield near-optimal theoretical guarantees. We apply our methodology to heart transplant allocation to develop theoretically grounded policies based on structural properties of historical data. Furthermore, in simulations based on real data, our policy closely matches the performance of the omniscient benchmark, achieving competitive ratio 0.91, drastically higher than the US status quo policy's 0.51. Our work bridges the gap between data-driven heuristics and pessimistic theoretical lower bounds.
